questions.q: Why does the orchestration layer persist each iteration's job state rather than only keeping it in memory?
options: So that if the process restarts mid-run, it can resume from the last completed iteration instead of silently restarting the whole 80-iteration loop and re-incurring cost for already-completed work
Persisted state is required by every cloud quantum provider's terms of service
Persisting state makes the QPU execute circuits faster
In-memory state is technically impossible to implement for quantum jobs
questions.explain: Without persisted state, a crash or restart would lose track of which iterations already completed, risking a costly full re-run -- persisted state enables resuming exactly where the run left off.

questions.q: For this project's 6-parameter ansatz, how many circuit evaluations make up one iteration's batched program-set submission?
options: 13 (6 parameters x 2 shifts + 1 cost evaluation), all submitted as one batched job
1, since batching reduces it to a single evaluation
80, matching the total iteration count
6, one per parameter only
questions.explain: Following the parameter-shift formula (2 x params + 1), a 6-parameter ansatz needs 13 evaluations per iteration, all bundled into one program-set submission rather than 13 separate ones.

questions.q: Why does the orchestration layer poll job status on a scheduled interval rather than blocking in a tight while-loop?
options: Scheduled polling is required because QPUs cannot be polled more than once
Blocking loops are faster, but scheduled polling is required by law
There is no real difference; the choice is purely cosmetic
It matches the non-blocking pattern from the orchestration chapter, which scales to running multiple concurrent jobs (e.g., multiple molecules) later without a rewrite
questions.explain: A blocking loop ties up the process for the full queue wait and doesn't scale to handling multiple concurrent jobs. Scheduled polling, as established in the orchestration lesson, supports future scaling without a rewrite.

questions.q: What does the classical optimizer actually receive from the orchestration layer after a submission completes and is aggregated?
options: Only the aggregated (value, standard error) pair -- never the raw per-circuit measurement counts
The raw measurement counts dictionary directly, with no aggregation
The full job state machine history for all 80 iterations
The device's queue depth and calibration metadata
questions.explain: The optimizer is kept decoupled from quantum-specific data formats, consuming only the aggregated (value, stderr) pair computed by the shot-weighted aggregation logic -- the same separation-of-concerns principle from the Pre/Post-Processing Lab.

questions.q: Why does the orchestration layer run the full 80-iteration loop against a classical simulator before ever submitting to Rigetti Ankaa-3?
options: To confirm the optimizer converges and the state machine correctly handles an injected failure at effectively zero cost, before spending any real money on hardware -- directly applying the 'develop against a simulator first' fix from Chapter 1
Because the simulator produces a more accurate result than real hardware would
Because real hardware cannot run more than a few iterations without failing
Because simulators are mandatory for any quantum job under provider terms of service
questions.explain: This directly applies the Chapter 1 fix for Mistake 1 (developing against real hardware): verifying the full loop's logic (convergence, failure handling) on a free simulator first avoids paying real-hardware prices to debug code that isn't even correct yet.
